El agua pura tiene pH 7, pero la lluvia: Pure water has pH 7, but rain is never pure water: as it falls it dissolves CO₂ from the air, which forms carbonic acid, a weak acid: $CO_2 + H_2O ⇌ H_2CO_3 ⇌ H^+ + HCO_3^−$.\n\nWith 420 ppm of CO₂, $1.4·10^{−5} "mol/L"$ dissolve, and with $K_a = 4.3·10^{−7}$ the acid dissociates little: solving the equilibrium, $[H^+] = ${f2(datos.h0 * 1e6)}·10^{−6} "M"$ and $pH = ${f2(datos.ph0)}$. That is normal: only rain below 5.6 is called acid rain.

El carbón y el gasóleo llevan algo de az: Coal and diesel contain some sulphur, which when burned gives sulphur dioxide: $S + O_2 → SO_2$. And in engines and power stations, at such high temperature, the nitrogen in the air reacts with oxygen and forms nitrogen oxides, NOₓ.\n\nTall chimneys carry them far: acid rain usually falls hundreds of kilometres from where it was emitted, sometimes in another country.

En el aire, con el oxígeno, la luz y las: In the air, with oxygen, light and cloud droplets, SO₂ ends up as sulphuric acid, $SO_2 + 1/2 O_2 + H_2O → H_2SO_4$, and NOₓ as nitric acid, $HNO_3$. Both are strong acids: they dissociate completely.\n\nWith just ${SULF} µmol/L of $H_2SO_4$, which gives two $H^+$ each, $[H^+] ≈ 2 · 3·10^{−5} = 6·10^{−5} "M"$ and the pH drops to ${f2(datos.phAcida)}. Now carbonic acid no longer counts: the strong acid rules.

De pH ${f1(datos.ph0)} a ${f1(datos.phAc: From pH ${f1(datos.ph0)} to ${f1(datos.phAcida)} it seems a small difference, but each pH unit multiplies the $H^+$ by 10: $10^{${f2(datos.ph0)} − ${f2(datos.phAcida)}} ≈ ${Math.round(datos.veces)}$.\n\nAcid rain washes away the nutrients in the soil and damages the leaves of fir trees; in lakes, below pH 5, trout and their eggs die. And it dissolves the marble and limestone of statues and cathedrals: $CaCO_3 + H_2SO_4 → CaSO_4 + CO_2 + H_2O$.

Un lago sobre roca caliza tiene bicarbon: A lake on limestone rock has dissolved bicarbonate, which eats up the $H^+$ that arrives: $HCO_3^− + H^+ → H_2CO_3$. With its carbonic acid it forms a buffer solution, and its pH comes from Henderson-Hasselbalch: $pH = pK_a + log([HCO_3^−]/[H_2CO_3]) = 6.37 + log(10^{−3}/10^{−4}) = ${f2(datos.lagoAntes)}$.\n\nIf $6·10^{−6} "mol/L"$ of $H^+$ arrives, the ratio becomes $(10^{−3} − 6·10^{−6})/(10^{−4} + 6·10^{−6})$ and the pH barely drops, to ${f2(datos.lagoDespues)}. In a lake on granite, with no buffer, the same acid would leave it at ${f1(datos.aguaPura)}. That is why Scandinavia suffered so much: almost everything is granite.
en el mar desde 1850: su pH ha bajado de: in the sea since 1850: its pH has dropped from 8.2 to 8.1.
El mar absorbe una cuarta parte del CO₂: The sea absorbs a quarter of the CO₂ we emit. When it dissolves it forms carbonic acid, and the pH of the sea, which is basic, has dropped from 8.2 to 8.1: it seems little, but it is $10^{0.1} − 1 = ${Math.round(100 * datos.masH)} %$ more $H^+$.\n\nThe sea is buffered by bicarbonate and carbonate, and to slow the change it uses up carbonate: $CO_3^{2−} + H^+ → HCO_3^−$. That carbonate is what corals, clams and plankton use to make their shells. The good news: SO₂ in Europe has fallen more than 90 % since 1980 thanks to filters on chimneys and sulphur-free diesel.
